47864.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse reiðr (“roadstead, anchorage”), from Middle Low German rēde (“roadstead, anchorage”) and reide (“roadstead, anchorage”).

en.g: a fortiori; with stronger or greater reason, as a conclusion following with even greater force from an already accepted premise
x: Hvis dette gjelder i det mindre tilfellet, gjelder det a fortiori i det større.
If this applies in the lesser case, it applies a fortiori in the greater one.
Norge … har vært forpliktet til ikke å bestride den danske suverenitet over hele Grønland og à fortiori til å avholde sig fra å okkupere en del av landet
Norway … has been obliged not to contest Danish sovereignty over the whole of Greenland and a fortiori to refrain from occupying part of the country.

1000440.etyen:
Unadapted borrowing from Medieval Latin ā fortiōrī (“from a stronger reason”).
The first element, ā (“from, by”), is a form of ab (“from, away from”), inherited from Proto-Italic *ap (“off, away”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó (“off, away”).
The second element, fortiōrī (“stronger”), is the ablative singular of fortior (“stronger”), the comparative of fortis (“strong, powerful”), from Proto-Italic *forktis (“strong, powerful”). Its further Proto-Indo-European origin is uncertain.
The Medieval Latin expression is an ellipsis of ā fortiōrī ratiōne, literally “from a stronger reason”, referrin

1001976.etyen:
For the upper-class sense, an unadapted borrowing from English high life (“upper-class life”). The musical sense is from English highlife (“West African musical genre”), itself from the same expression. First attested before 1845.
Compare the parallel borrowings Danish highlife, Swedish high life, German Highlife, French high-life and Polish high life (“upper-class life; high society”).

en.g: a triquetra; a three-part interconnected figure consisting of overlapping or interlaced arcs, loops, triangles, or similar forms, used as an ornament, symbol, or protective mark
x: Trikvetraen var et sentralt motiv på flere norske middelaldermynter.
The triquetra was a central motif on several Norwegian medieval coins.

1004536.etyen:
Borrowed from Latin triquetra (“three-cornered, triangular”), the feminine singular of triquetrus (“three-cornered, triangular”), probably through the phrase triquetra figura (“three-cornered figure”). The adjective is formed from tri- (“three”) and an element meaning “pointed, cornered”, perhaps ultimately related to *kʷeh₁d- (“to sharpen”).
Compare Swedish trikvetra, Danish trikvetra, German Triqueta (also Triquetta and Triquetra)

en.g: a farm in Kolbu, Østre Toten, Innlandet, Norway
a surname from habitational, from the Norwegian smallholding of the same name in Kolbu, Østre Toten

1004792.etyen: The place name is of uncertain origin. The surname is habitational, from Skolby, a smallholding under Mellom-Gran in Kolbu, Østre Toten. The name is documented in connection with residents of the smallholding by 1906.

en.g: deplorable, regrettable, lamentable; deserving or arousing regret
x: De er en beklagelsesværdig kvinde, fru Alving.
You are a deplorable woman, Mrs. Alving.

1005048.etyen:
Compound of beklagelse (“regret; apology; complaint”) + verdig (“worthy”), with linking -s- (“interfix”), literally “worthy of regret”.
Compare Danish beklagelsesværdig (“deplorable, regrettable”), Swedish beklagansvärd (“deplorable, regrettable”), German beklagenswert (“deplorable, regrettable”) and Dutch beklagenswaardig (“lamentable, pitiful”).
